column5: trembling at the divine word
column6: The commentary makes inward reverent fear the condition for receiving the reminder; Isaiah says God regards the humble, contrite person who trembles at his word.

column5: hearing the Torah to learn fear
column6: After the command to remind listeners, this assembly is told to hear and learn to fear YHWH, making reception of instruction a cultivated inner response.

column5: tender heart hearing the book
column6: Josiah's heart is tender and he humbles himself when he hears the judgment read; the response depends on the hearer's disposition, as the commentary says the reminder works in the one who fears.

column5: those fearing YHWH and a book of remembrance
column6: Those who fear YHWH speak together, are heard, and have a memorial written before God; this joins the commentary's inward fear to its account of remembering and preserving what might otherwise be lost.

column5: memorial stones leading to fear
column6: The stones recall Israel's crossing so peoples know YHWH's strong hand and Israel fears him always, concretely linking retained memory with reverent fear.

column5: remembering the wilderness and testing the heart
column6: Israel is told to remember the wilderness way because the testing disclosed what was in its heart and whether it would keep the command; recollection and inward orientation meet as in the commentary.

column5: children hear and learn to fear
column6: The children who have not known the Torah are to hear and learn fear of YHWH, showing that the decisive response is acquired by the hearer rather than inherited as a group label.

column5: Noah fears concerning what is not yet seen
column6: Warned about events still unseen, Noah acts in reverent fear and saves his household; this gives a concrete instance of fear before sight prompting a timely response.

column5: word held fast in a good heart
column6: The hearers with an honest, good heart hold the word fast and bear fruit with endurance, closely matching the commentary's claim that the listener, not the messenger, must take the reminder inwardly.

column5: the hearer who forgets versus the doer
column6: James contrasts a hearer who forgets with one who perseveres in the law and acts; it makes explicit the commentary's movement from recovering what slipped away to a changed response.

column5: fear of God and doing righteousness in every nation
column6: Peter says that in every nation the person who fears God and does righteousness is acceptable to him, concretely shifting the criterion from ancestry to the inward posture and conduct emphasized in the commentary.

column5: fear, glory, judgment, and worship of the Creator
column6: The angel commands fear of God and giving him glory because judgment has arrived, then calls for worship of the Creator; this joins reverence to creation and worship as the commentary's surah does.

column5: worship with reverence and awe
column6: The community is to offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe; the next verse grounds this in God as consuming fire, giving the commentary's fear-to-prayer movement a concrete Christian formulation.

column5: fear of the one with authority after death
column6: Jesus redirects fear from human killers to the one who has authority after death, specifying a future, unseen consequence where the Qur'anic verse leaves the object of fear unstated.

column5: the Spirit bringing Jesus' words to remembrance
column6: Jesus promises that the Spirit will teach and remind the disciples of what he said; this parallels the commentary's concern with future recollection while locating its source in divine aid.

column5: remembering after the judgment has begun
column6: Abraham tells the rich man to remember his former life after the chasm is fixed; the memory is real but cannot repair the missed opportunity, like the commentary's late remembrance after Gehenna is brought.

column5: recollection after the teacher's departure
column6: Peter makes provision for his readers to recall his teaching after his death, a specific case of a messenger's reminder becoming the hearer's future act of memory.

column5: remembering the prior saying after a reminder
column6: At the tomb the women remember Jesus' earlier words after the messengers call them to remember; the scene distinguishes the spoken reminder from the hearers' act of recollection.

column5: understanding remembered later
column6: The disciples first fail to understand the events, then remember Jesus' words after his glorification; this supplies a delayed, retrospective counterpart to the commentary's expected near-future remembrance.

column5: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
column6: The commentary labels the Arabic root ذ ك ر; Deuteronomy uses its Hebrew cognate זכר for remembering YHWH as the giver of Israel's power, recalling dependence rather than crediting oneself.

column5: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכרון
column6: The commentary labels ذ ك ر for remembering; Joshua calls the stones a זכרון, a memorial of the crossing, so a retained sign carries the past forward and leads in verse 24 to fear.

column5: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
column6: The commentary's Arabic root label is ذ ك ر; the psalm uses Hebrew זכר for remembering God's precepts and doing them, joining memory to enacted obedience.

column5: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
column6: The commentary labels Arabic ذ ك ر; Exodus uses Hebrew זכר of God remembering his covenant and responding to Israel's groaning, a divine answer that contrasts with the hearer's own work of recollection.

column5: fear of YHWH as the beginning of knowledge
column6: Proverbs makes fear of YHWH the beginning of knowledge and contrasts it with despising instruction; this links the commentary's knowledge-laden fear to readiness to receive a reminder.

column5: fear and turning from evil as wisdom
column6: Job identifies fear of the Lord with wisdom and turning from evil with understanding, connecting reverence to both knowing and a changed course.

column5: fear placed before Israel to restrain sin
column6: At Sinai Moses says the divine testing is meant to put fear before Israel so they do not sin; fear is an apprehension of divine presence that shapes what the hearer does.

column5: steadfast mercy toward those who fear YHWH
column6: The psalm describes enduring mercy as belonging to those who fear YHWH, then the next verse describes covenant-keepers who remember his commands; the two verses join inward reverence to active remembrance.

column5: serving with fear and trembling
column6: The rulers are told to serve YHWH with fear and rejoice with trembling, a concrete route from reverence to worship that complements the commentary's later movement toward prayer.

column5: forgiveness followed by fear
column6: The psalm says forgiveness is with God so that he may be feared, reversing the commentary's main order of fear leading to remembrance and showing a distinct scriptural sequence.

column5: fear placed in hearts so they will not turn away
column6: God promises to put fear in the people's hearts to keep them from turning away; this gives the disposition a divine source, sharpening the commentary's account of listener agency within God's will.

column5: lips honor while the heart is far away
column6: Isaiah condemns a fear of God taught as human precept when the heart remains distant, a precise warning against treating outward religious speech as the inward fear that receives the reminder.

column5: fear and belief after Israel sees the deliverance
column6: Israel sees YHWH's great power, then fears and believes; unlike the commentary's person who fears before seeing, this places fear after visible deliverance and makes the difference in timing clear.

column5: warning those who forget God
column6: The psalm warns those who forget God to consider their end before there is no rescuer; it concretizes the commentary's contrast between pursuing what has slipped away and suffering the loss of it.

column5: counsel and covenant knowledge for those who fear
column6: The psalm says YHWH shares his counsel with those who fear him and makes his covenant known to them, linking reverence with knowledge rather than treating fear as uncomprehending panic.

column5: conduct in fear before the impartial judge
column6: Peter tells believers to conduct themselves in fear during their exile because God judges each person's work impartially; the fear is tied to knowledge of a real future reckoning.

column5: holiness brought to completion in fear of God
column6: Paul urges cleansing from defilement and completion of holiness in fear of God, connecting reverence to the purification that the commentary places after remembrance.

column5: working out salvation with fear and trembling
column6: Paul calls the community to act with fear and trembling, then says God is at work in them; this holds human response together with divine action as the commentary does for the listener's open door.

column5: fear as the opposite of prideful self-assurance
column6: Paul says branches were broken off through unbelief and warns the standing branch not to become proud but to fear; this gives a specific counterpart to the commentary's self-sufficient hearer who sees no need to recover anything.

column5: fear of punishment cast out by perfected love
column6: John says fear has to do with punishment and is cast out by perfected love; this distinguishes punitive dread from the commentary's reverential fear instead of making the two senses identical.

column5: remembering generations while fearing the Lord
column6: Ben Sira tells those who fear the Lord to look at generations past and asks who trusted him and was forsaken; remembered precedent supports trust, joining memory and reverence in one argument.

column5: fear of sin preceding wisdom
column6: The Mishnah says wisdom endures when fear of sin precedes it; this directly parallels the commentary's ordering of an inward fear before the act of remembering and receiving instruction.

column5: wisdom and fear as reciprocal conditions
column6: The Mishnah says that without wisdom there is no fear and without fear there is no wisdom, preserving both directions of the relationship that the commentary illustrates with fear leading to remembrance and remembrance sometimes awakening fear.

column5: what is in Heaven's hand and fear of Heaven
column6: The Talmud says all is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven; the commentary, citing the Qur'anic qualification that remembrance depends on God's will, keeps the listener's response inside divine willing, making their accounts of agency diverge.

column5: fear of God distinguished from fear of the devil
column6: Hermas urges fear of God and says this displaces fear of the devil, distinguishing reverent accountability from panic and giving a concrete early Christian account of fear directing conduct.
